I am here this evening to speak about collective bargaining based on both what the research states and briefly regarding my own personal experience growing up in a union household in Philadelphia.

My household growing up was comprised of six people, my father, stepmother, brother, two sisters, and myself. My father was a union sheet metal worker and my stepmother was a homemaker, generating no financial revenue for our household. We were not living large by any means, but we owned our modest twin home, two used vehicles, went on one vacation a year, had clothes that fit, bills that were paid, and three meals a day.

All of this with no college education and one income. The first Monday of every month, my father would travel downtown to attend his union meeting, and as a brotherhood, they would voice their concerns and demand livable wages, benefits, and decent working conditions, resulting in a high-quality workforce, high quality work around the city of Philadelphia and union members who could take care of their families.

My husband and I as two college educated, experienced educators would not be able to replicate the same. Overwhelmingly, the data show that collective bargaining strengthens schools. Here are just a few of the benefits in education for the 44 states in this country who negotiate with their educators.

Collective bargaining prevents teacher burnout, which is one of the main reasons why 44% of teachers leave the field within five years. Highly unionized divisions dismiss more low-quality teachers and retain high-quality ones collective bargaining leads to adequate wages improved working conditions and dignified terms of employment for all school staff including food service workers counselors libraries librarians office staff and custodians it improves staff retention and student achievement and improves student test scores across all income levels collective bargaining leads to more school programs not a cut to them allowing more students to spend time in enriching environments it leads to more

critical support staff enables the democratic process in the forms of problem-solving and decision-making with the staff who are closest to the ground and know best what students need to succeed currently low pay challenging working conditions and inadequate support are driving teacher and staff turnover and harming our students in just the last month at Dean alone we have lost a second grade teacher a third grade teacher and a sped teacher collapsed a first and second grade class dispersing those students among other classes three-fourths of the way into the year and have been pulling our instructional assistants daily from their kindergarten classrooms to cover other assignments and shortages throughout the building our children are

suffering the consequences if teachers and support staff could have a seat at the table we can speak with a more powerful voice to raise teacher and staff pay increase retention improve working conditions and boost teacher morale we would be able to retain experienced highly high-quality teachers and staff who can make the most difference in the lives of the children we serve. After all, our working conditions are our students' learning conditions. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Cook. Heather DiNardo. Heather DiNardo. Good evening. My name is

good evening chairman Seberg and school board members my name is Shaniqua Williams and I serve the students at Metz middle school as one of the school counselors I also reside in the Brentsville district in Prince William County when leadership pushes out misinformation it creates an environment of mistrust and uncertainty people begin to question not only the the accuracy of what's being told,

but the integrity of those that are in charge. Trust is the foundation of any successful organization, and once it's been broken, it's incredibly difficult to rebuild. When employees feel disconnected from leadership or believe their leaders are not being honest, morale suffers, frustration builds, engagement declines, and the workplace culture shifts to one where people feel unheard and undervalued.

A loss in trust leads to a loss of motivation and commitment, making it harder for everyone to work towards our common goal. I may not know you personally, but I want to believe your heart is in the right place and that you're committed to speaking from a place of truth, knowledge, and not your opinions.

Leadership carries the responsibility of ensuring that information is accurate and transparent because your words have power. When misinformation is spread, it does more than mislead. It creates division, frustration, and a sense of betrayal, and we see those consequences in our world every single day.

I urge you to always choose integrity, to value truth over convenience, because that is what builds a strong, united, respected leadership team. When employees can trust their leaders, they feel supported, engaged, and motivated to give their best.

But when that trust is broken, morale crumbles, and the entire organization suffers. Leadership is not just about making decisions, it's about fostering trust, and that starts with honesty. Thank you very much. - Thank you, Ms. Williams.
Anna Demeria. - Hi, good evening. I'm Anna Demeria, I am a fourth grade teacher at Baldwin Elementary School, but I am also the proud president of the Manasseh Education Association.

Collective bargaining is the cornerstone that drives the success of our schools, students, and the committed educators who shape its future. It's about more than negotiating wages or contract terms. It's about fostering an environment where everyone in the school community, from teachers to food service workers, from counselors to custodians can thrive.

When our school staff succeed, our students succeed. It is that simple. Research consistently shows that collective bargaining strengthens our schools when educators have a voice in shaping their working conditions and has a direct, positive impact on student learning.

Educators who work in safe, well-resourced environments are better able to focus on what matters most. providing the best education possible for their students. Stronger educators lead to stronger students. But let's be clear, collective bargaining isn't just about improving conditions for teachers, it's about improving the learning environment for all students.

Teachers, as we know, are the heart of the classroom. They want the same things every family wants. Smaller class sizes, better technology, more programs, and more support staff. These are the essentials that create richer, more meaningful educational experiences for every student.

Moreover, collective bargaining is not just for teachers, it's for support staff too, who play an integral role in the functioning of our schools. Each member of the school community, whether they teach, support, or maintain the building, is essential for our students' success.

Collective bargaining ensures that everyone has a seat at the table to advocate for their needs. When all parts of the school community come together, we all benefit. My name is Kristen Watley, and I am the lead speech-language pathologist for Manassas City Public Schools I'm speaking to you tonight regarding the proposed budget and staffing of SLPs for the for the upcoming school year Approximately 10% of MCPS students from preschool through high school qualify for special education services of those 788 students

Approximately 44% of them receive speech-language therapy services that are provided by only seven SLPs. For the past several years, the SLPs have needed to work in other buildings besides our base schools due to insufficient staffing.

Often we need to make adjustments to our caseloads and school assignments in order to keep from exceeding the maximum allowable caseload for SLPs. Being split between buildings limits our ability to effectively collaborate with our colleagues. We also lose critical instructional time while traveling between buildings.

Our students deserve continuity and consistency in therapy services so they can make progress with their communication skills. The duties of the SLPs extend far beyond providing speech language therapy services. We are required to complete screenings and evaluations, attend eligibility and IEP meetings, and complete special education paperwork within legally required compliance deadlines.

We spend nearly all of our time working directly with students, so we do not have sufficient time during the school day to complete required paperwork. Therefore, we are constantly working on paperwork outside of our contract hours. MCPS currently has six full-time SLPs and one contracted SLP.

For many years, we have been unsuccessful in attempts to fill vacant SLP positions. We've only had a few applicants, and we've lost new hires to other school divisions due to our lower salary scale and higher caseloads. SLPs have left MCPS to work in private practice or in other school districts, where they now receive higher compensation with smaller caseloads and more manageable workloads.

We have resorted to hiring contracted SLPs to cover staffing shortages for the last several years. This short-term solution is not sustainable or fiscally responsible since contracted SLP salaries are significantly higher than the average salary of our full-time SLPs.

All of our SLPs have master's degrees, are nationally certified through ASHA, and are licensed through the Virginia Board of Audiology and Speech Pathology. I ask you to ensure that the proposed salary scale for the SLPs is reflective of the highly specialized nature of our jobs.
We need to have a competitive salary and benefits package along with a reasonable workload so we can recoup and retain our highly qualified speech pass. Thank you. - Thank you, Ms. Watley.

Public Schools this summer we will be expanding programs for students at the elementary intermediate and middle levels to kindergarten through eighth grade at multiple locations the elementary students will be served at Baldwin Elementary and the intermediate and middle school students will be served at Mayfield intermediate school these programs will be held from June 23rd to July 10th and will run Monday through Thursday hours will be 8:30 a.m.

to noon at both Baldwin and at Mayfield we will be targeting an enrollment range of 60 to 90 total students per grade level in these programs which will give us a student to teacher ratio of between 15 and 20 to 1 this will result in the staffing and materials cost of about three hundred and ten dollars per classroom per day the structure of this year's K through 8 summer school will be similar to the 2024 program, which provided a combination of direct literacy instruction and support with opportunities to apply skills through cross-disciplinary learning exploration.

The program's goal will be to extend and strengthen the phonological, comprehension, oral language, and writing skills that students built during the school year. The program will utilize the new core and intervention literacy resources established in our school division under the Virginia Literacy Act this year.

These resources provide tools for measuring student growth that can be used to inform instructional decisions around individual student support needs during summer school and help evaluate the program's effectiveness in meeting the overall goal of extending and strengthening student foundational literacy skills.

Because these tools exist inside of our core and intervention programs, the data will also be available to schools and teachers in the fall. In addition to direct literacy instruction, students will also spend time applying their literacy skills in different content areas through learning exploration activities of varying lengths and varieties.

And an informal learning showcase will be held on the last day of summer school to give the students and community members an opportunity to share and celebrate the sessions learning. Osborne High School will host our summer programs for students in grades 9 through 12.

These programs will run from June 16th to July 24th from 8:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. They will also target a 15 to 20 student class size with an overall anticipated participation rate of between 200 and 250 students. Dates and times for the high school sports camps are in the process of being scheduled due to the gym resurfacing at Osborne. We are about to move into high gear for summer program planning. We are beginning recruiting earlier this year to put us in the best possible position to fully staff all planned grades.

We will be working with our schools to ensure invitations to our core programs are sent out to our highest needs students based on literacy and language data in the coming month. Schools will follow up with the parents of those who do not respond to invitations and those who turn them down to make sure they are fully aware of the benefits of this program before extending additional invitations to families as needed.

In May, we will be finalizing program logistics to include transportation and student information system set up ahead of sending pre-programmed communications to parents of participating families. We have planned multiple days the week before the first day of school for teacher training and for setup. I am now pleased to turn things over to Brian Maciak, our Director of Special Education, for details on our extended school year programming. Good evening, Chair Seberg, Vice Chair Spall,

School Board members, and Mr. Gefeller. It is my pleasure to present information to you about our extended school year programming. I would like to start this evening's presentation with an overview of the qualification criteria for ESY services.

This determination is made by an IEP team in an IEP meeting. Most often, there is sufficient data to make this determination at the annual IEP meeting. At times, the IEP team may choose to make the determination at a later date after more data has been collected.
The overarching question that determines qualification for ESY is, would the gains a student made during the regular school year be significantly jeopardized if the student does not receive ESY?

As teams consider this question, they look at several factors in supporting data, and these factors include regression and recoupment, the degree of progress, emerging skills in breakthrough opportunities, interfering behaviors, the nature and severity of the disability, or special circumstances or other factors.
Our traditional ESY program is a classroom-based program that's very much like the regular school year. Typically, our students on an adapted curriculum qualify for traditional ESY services.

Our traditional ESY program will run from June 23rd through July 10th, Monday through Thursday, Teacher hours, or student hours, excuse me, are from 8:30 to 11:30, while staff hours are from 8:00 to 12:00.

Just to give you a picture of what it looked like last year, our numbers in 23-24 break down like this. In early childhood special education, we had 11 students who qualified across two classrooms, and that was held at Dean Elementary.

Our school-aged children in grades K through five, we had 23 students who qualified, and they were spread among three classrooms, also housed at Dean Elementary. Our school-aged children in grades five through 12, there were 20 students who qualified, and they were spreading across two classrooms.

You may notice fifth grade was listed more than once. We use that as a buffer grade, so we can balance our loads at the schools. We can either put them with the elementary, or the secondary, or sometimes even split them just to balance our loads at the schools a little bit.

Our locations for 24, 25 don't look a whole lot different. The only thing we will be doing at Dean this year is our early childhood programs. My early childhood teachers, I love them. They got lots of stuff and I don't wanna move it. There's lots of stuff and we, so we're gonna limit what we do at Dean this year because of all the wonderful construction and good things that are going on over there.

So our school-aged children's grades K through five will be housed on the Baldwin campus and our school-aged children grades five through 12 will be housed on the Mayfield campus, which is the same as it was last year.
